item.title: Vance says US, S. Korea still need to 'work out' details of Alaska gas project
item.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday the United States and South Korea still need to "work out" details of a proposed liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska, while expressing confidence that the project will ultimately move forward amid strong Asian demand for American gas. "The pipeline is something that we really want to see happen and a lot of our Asian friends want to happen as well," Vance said, according to a White House pool report. "It's not just the South Koreans. The Japanese would love to see this pipeline." "So I think it's something that's going to happen," he said. "Obviously, you still got to work out some of the details and the South Koreans, you know, have spoken to that." Vance said East Asian economies that have faced higher natural gas prices would benefit from increased supplies of U.S. gas. "When there's a demand for this stuff and there really is strong demand for American natural gas, I think we're going to be able to get it done," he added. item.title: Iran president says talks with US 'meaningless': state media
item.description: TEHRAN — Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that negotiations with the United States were "meaningless" and only resulted in renewed attacks, state media reported, with progress on ending the Middle East war stalled for months. "So far, they have attacked us three times after talks, and this shows that they are not seeking dialogue; rather, their goal is to overthrow the Islamic Republic of Iran," Pezeshkian was quoted as saying by the state news agency IRNA. "With an enemy that every day resorts to assassination, sanctions, pressure and threats, and that breaks its commitments, negotiations are meaningless." The Middle East war was started in late February by the U.S. and Israel when they launched a wave of surprise attacks on Iran, even as Washington and Tehran were in the midst of negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme. The warring parties agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution to the conflict, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz prompted a return to U.S. military operations. Negotiations

item.title: 'Reckless' AI firms can't control models, says whistleblower
item.description: NEW YORK — Leading artificial intelligence companies do not know how to keep AI systems from pursuing objectives their developers did not assign, whistleblower Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI and Anthropic employee, warned Monday. "Companies are being extremely reckless given the stakes," Coxon told local lawmakers at a hearing before the New York City Council. In early September, the British researcher published a statement on X explaining his decision to resign from Anthropic, saying AI developers sincerely believed the technology could "kill us all by the end of the decade." His testimony made headlines around the world, and several current and former employees of AI's major players have since voiced similar concerns. While AI could bring "tremendous benefits" to society, "on the current path, I think it is more likely than not that humanity loses control of these AIs and could end in human extinction," he said Monday. "We don't know how to prevent them from developing goals of their own," beyond their creators' control, Coxon explained, "and we don't have the safeguards to prevent them

item.title: Mexico sends troops after US says shots fired across border
item.description: MEXICO CITY — Mexico has deployed 500 soldiers to its border with Texas after the United States reported U.S. personnel coming under gunfire, President Claudia Sheinbaum said Monday. The troops were posted in Tamaulipas state in an area wher the rival Northeast and Gulf drug cartels are fighting for control. The United States classified both as foreign terrorist organizations in February 2025. In her routine morning press conference, Sheinbaum said the United States reported that it took "shots from the Mexican border." But she added that the Trump administration provided no evidence. Mexico offered a troop deployment anyway along the Rio Grande, she said. U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson wrote on X that U.S. Coast Guard personnel "were fired upon." He said the newly deployed Mexican troops will communicate directly with U.S. forces. "Together, we intend to patrol both sides of our shared border, protect our communities, and make it more difficult for criminal and terrorist organizations to operate," Johnson wrote. item.title: Ex-USFK commander warns time-based OPCON transfer could weaken deterrence against N. Korea
item.description: WASHINGTON — A former commander of U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) warned Monday that hastening the transfer of wartime operational control (OPCON) to South Korea by setting an arbitrary timeline could increase security risks and weaken the allies' deterrence capabilities against North Korea. Retired Gen. Robert Abrams, who led USFK from 2018-21, made the remarks during a webinar hosted by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, as he discussed the allies' long-running efforts to transfer wartime OPCON from Washington to Seoul. "From my perspective and experience, I think there's a lot of risk that hasn't been properly been explained to everyone about hastening this (OPCON transfer) and putting it on a timeline," Abrams said. "Time-based fundamentally just increases risk and the risk is because there's still going to be operational shortfalls on the ROK military side," Abrams said, referring to South Korea by the acronym of its official name, the Republic of Korea. Abrams stressed that Seoul and Washington "need to make sure that we have sufficient force and capab

item.title: Students protest Cornell's response to gang rape complaint
item.description: ITHACA, New York — Cornell students thronged a campus plaza to protest the university's response to allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity house, and the school's main administration building was splashed with graffiti and damaged overnight. At a demonstration that overflowed the large space in front of the school's student center, students, faculty members and others wore purple ribbons and held signs with such messages as “support survivors, expel rapists” and “Justice 4 every Jane Doe" — the name by which the woman who reported the assault is known in court papers. Others watched from pathways, windows, and a nearby hill. “Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support,” student Athena Holloway told the crowd. “How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?” Hispanic studies professor Julia Chang added to applause: “Rape should not be inevitable.” Speakers faulted fraternities, the university trustees and Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff, saying he and his administrat

item.title: Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt lands her next gig: Fox News contributor
item.description: NEW YORK — Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has found her next chapter: She is heading to Fox News. Leavitt will serve as an on-air contributor beginning Nov. 1, the network said Monday. “Karoline’s firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today’s political landscape,” said the network’s CEO, Suzanne Scott. For her part, Leavitt, in the same statement, said she looked forward “to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House Press Secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defined my tenure, to Fox’s millions of viewers across their many platforms.” Leavitt, now 29, was the youngest person to hold the role of press secretary. When she left at the end of August, President Donald Trump described her as one of his “most trusted aides.” At the time she said she wanted to spend more time with her two children. Her second child, Viviana, was born in May, and she has a two-year-old son. Leavitt is not the first of Trump's press secretaries to join Fox

item.title: Nasdaq hits record high as investors focus on earnings
item.description: The Nasdaq hit an all-time high on Monday, lifted by Nvidia and Microsoft, as investors focused on a dip in oil prices and looked ahead to quarterly earnings reports. It was the Nasdaq's second straight intraday record high after weaker-than-expected jobs data on Friday dampened expectations for an interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve at its policy meeting this month. The S&P 500 climbed and was about 0.5 percent below its intraday record high on August 13. AI heavyweight Nvidia rose 1.6 percent, while Microsoft added 1.5 percent. Meta Platforms added 2.1 percent and Tesla climbed 2.5 percent. Oil prices slipped after crude exports from the Middle East increased and the Group of Seven nations pledged to boost supplies. "With the economic data calendar being light and earnings about a week away, investors are really groping for anything positive to glom onto, and clearly they're looking at lower energy prices," said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. item.title: US to announce $150 mil. for Alaska power lines as Vance campaigns in Senate battleground
item.description: ABOARD AIR FORCE TWO — The U.S. Energy Department will announce $150 million in new funding for power lines in Alaska on Monday as Vice President JD Vance visits the state, where Republicans are fighting to hold a critical Senate seat in the November midterm elections. Vance is set to rally voters for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a tight reelection battle with Democrat Mary Peltola. Flipping the seat is key to the Democratic Party's strategy to take control of the U.S. Senate, and recent polls have Peltola, a former member of the U.S. House of Representatives, leading Sullivan. The energy plan is the latest in a series of economic and investment announcements President Donald Trump and his administration have highlighted ahead of the midterms amid voter concerns over the Iran war and high gasoline prices. item.title: Top diplomat Rubio says US monitoring Siberia plague institute death
item.description: WASHINGTON — The United States is closely monitoring the case involving a laboratory worker who died at a plague research institute in Siberia, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday. "We're watching and monitoring it closely," Rubio told reporters before leaving for a trip to Europe. "I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause just to keep an eye on it." A laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people, and the head of Russia's health watchdog to fly to the region. There were conflicting reports about how and where the laboratory worker, whose age was given as 28, had fallen ill, but the authorities said she had died of pneumonia. item.title: Russia reports worker at Siberian plague institute got pneumonia from unknown cause and died
item.description: Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring contacts of an employee at a plague research institute in Siberia who contracted pneumonia of an “unknown” cause. Local state TV said the woman died last week. Russian authorities said they found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with. But the case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person. The woman worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, southeastern Siberia. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported Monday that she died last week in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk. The hospital has been placed under quarantine, Mayor Maxim Modin said Friday, no longer admitting or discharging patients, and its laboratory halted carrying out routine tests. The hospital's outpatient clinic kept operating as usual, he said. Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog,

item.description: “Bad, bad, bad….” At Jajaeam Temple, nestled deep in the valleys of Soyo Mountain in Dongducheon, Gyeonggi Province, the silence was broken by “BAD,” a popular song by boy band ATEEZ. The man engrossed in popping moves, his gray Buddhist robes flying around him, was Ven. Deoksan, the temple’s abbot. He shot to fame after dancing to G-Dragon and Taeyang’s “Good Boy” at a Buddhist Expo in April and Michael Jackson’s “Billie Jean” at the Lotus Lantern Festival in May. Despite being in his 60s, his unconventional dance moves have earned him colorful nicknames such as the “G-Dragon of Buddhism,” “Deoksan Daegong” and “Michael Jack-sunim,” a play on Michael Jackson and the Korean word for monk, “sunim.” Ven. item.title: "Incredible Moment for the Borderlands": Judge Blocks Border Wall Expansion in Big Bend & West Texas
item.description:
In a victory for environmentalists and immigration rights’ advocates, a federal judge in El Paso, Texas, has blocked further border wall construction inside Big Bend National Park. “We slammed the brakes on $7 billion worth of corrupt construction contracts,” says Laiken Jordahl, a national public lands advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity, which sued to block the expansion. “We have effectively stopped construction across West Texas, and it’s incredible.”

Jordahl also responds to the Trump administration’s excavation of a 200-year-old cottonwood tree on the Arizona-Mexico border that had been protected by activists for months. “Watching those videos of them toppling this ancient tree that was very likely older than the border itself is symbolic of how DHS has treated the border region. They see our communities, our wildlife, our nature as a sacrifice zone,” says Jordahl.

item.title: Ebola Death Toll in DRC Tops 4,000; Trump USAID Cuts Fuel Outbreak
item.description:
We go to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the site of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. Health authorities believe the outbreak first began in January but was not detected until May, in part due to cuts in global health investments, like the dismantling of USAID. Since then, over 8,000 cases have been recorded, with more than 4,000 fatalities so far. From Bunia, Ituri province, the epicenter of the outbreak, we speak to Congolese journalist Akilimali Chomachoma. Chomachoma describes the strain on the underfunded Congolese healthcare system as the disease spreads. Many frontline workers have not been paid for months.

“We are seeing this outbreak emerge, and really unfurl, in a setting of decreased global health support,” says Craig Spencer, a doctor and public health expert based in the United States who contracted Ebola while on a medical mission to Guinea in 2014. “The U.S. has not shown up in the same way that it has in previous Ebola outbreaks.” Spencer also comments on the “unprecedented” measles outbreak in the United States, which he warns is likely to continue and lead to additional deaths.

item.title: French High School Students Lead Mass Protests over School Funding, Inequality; Thousands Arrested
item.description:
Nearly 2,000 French high schools are blockaded or closed today amid massive student-led protests over school funding and inequality. The demonstrations began in September at a single school in the economically deprived suburbs of Paris, where students protested teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated school buildings beset by rats, falling debris and more. But the scope of the protests has widened amid a violent crackdown by French police. French authorities have arrested more than 5,000 people, largely underage students, since the movement began. Violent police tactics have led to serious injuries. One protester lost an eye after being hit by a rubber bullet, while another lost a hand when he picked up a police stun grenade.

We hear from an anonymous protester who describes the violence meted out on students, who “aren’t even adults yet,” and from Claire Vigneau, general secretary of Fédération Syndicale Étudiante, the French student union, who reports from a protest in Rennes, Brittany, “where we are trying to escape from the policemen that are chasing us with tear gas and with water cannon[s].”

“The amount of spending that France has done on education has stagnated, if not declined,” explains French American journalist Cole Stangler. “The critiques that high school students are making are actually very similar to what teachers’ unions have been saying for quite some time.”

“Everyone is deeply, deeply angry. We are completely fed up [with] the living conditions, the school conditions, the work conditions that we have,” says Alys Rowlands, a university student in Lille and also a member of Fédération Syndicale Étudiante. “The true violence is the violence of the state that we are being faced with all day, every day, all year. That’s the true violence: having no money, having difficulty finishing the month, having less and less help from the state, having to choose between eating and putting your heating on during the winter.”

item.title: From drought to deluge: ‘Super’ El Niño’s expanding reach

item.title: LG Electronics secures North American AI data center cooling deal
item.description: LG Electronics has signed a long-term supply agreement with AIR Control Concepts, a global platform for companies specializing in heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC), electrical, service and controls, to provide advanced chillers for data centers in the United States and Canada, the company said Monday. The deal covers large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) data center projects with a combined capacity of more than 5 gigawatts in North America, strengthening LG's position in the rapidly growing AI data center cooling market. AIR oversees large-scale infrastructure projects across major North American data center hubs and serves leading global data center operators. Under the agreement, LG will supply advanced chillers for AIR's data center projects. Its Air-Cooled Centrifugal Chiller for AI data centers incorporates refrigerant-free cooling technology that uses outdoor air to reduce the cooling load on compressors. item.description: Lisa Su, chief executive officer of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), will visit Korea this week to meet semiconductor industry executives and government officials, the company said Monday. The visit comes about seven months after Su's previous trip to Korea in March. item.title: German, US scientists win Nobel medicine prize for work on optogenetics
item.description: STOCKHOLM — American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for their discoveries on light and optogenetics that have helped understand how the brain works. The Nobel Assembly of Sweden's Karolinska Institute medical university said Deisseroth, 54, Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, were selected for their "discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics." Optogenetics "makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain," said Thomas Perlmann, Secretary-General of the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet. "This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries," Perlmann said. In clinical trials, researchers are restoring vision to people blinded by a condition called retinitis pigmentosa by inserting a light-sensitive protein in the retina. item.title: AI-powered attacks on banks expose technological lag in Korea's financial cyber defenses
item.description: Cyber defenses across Korea’s financial sector are facing intense scrutiny after a string of attacks hit banks and other financial companies, raising fears that artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyberattacks could outpace existing security measures. Seven financial firms have reported information leaks so far since Thursday, including three of the country’s largest commercial banks — Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and Hana Bank — along with Busan Bank, Yegaram Savings Bank, Welcome Savings Bank and Hyundai Capital. More than 67,000 people are believed to have been affected. The leaked information includes customers’ names, contact details, resident registration numbers, annual income and loan limits. AI-powered attacks The latest incidents differ from some of the biggest cybersecurity breaches in the past, when the core IT or transaction systems of individual institutions were compromised. This time, multiple firms were targeted in quick succession, with attackers apparently looking for easier ways in. The cyber criminals, believed to be based overseas, repeatedly probed less

item.title: Seoul concludes North Korea responsible for DMZ land mine explosions
item.description: South Korea’s military said Monday it has concluded that North Korean forces planted mines south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), in a violation of the 1953 Korean War Armistice Agreement. The conclusion, drawing on a joint on-site investigation with the United Nations Command (UNC) and forensic findings from the National Forensic Service, came about two weeks after the Sept. 21 land mine explosions injured three South Korean troops. The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said it carried out a mine-clearance operation in the area earlier in the day, demanding an apology from Pyongyang and warning that Seoul would continue removing North Korean mines south of the MDL unless the North clears the mines voluntarily. “In conclusion, based on the results of the joint investigation with the UNC and scientific evidence, we have determined that our troops conducting routine DMZ operations sustained serious injuries from North Korean plastic anti-personnel mines planted south of the MDL, under the pretext of North Korea’s so-called border-fortification work,

item.title: Korea begins US investment but trade pressure persists
item.description: Korea has begun implementing its $350 billion investment commitment in the United States, but U.S. pressure for additional investments and an ongoing review of unfair foreign trade practices are keeping Seoul on edge over the possibility of additional tariffs. Korea recently made its first $2.4 billion capital injection into the U.S., marking the first phase of the $350 billion investment package finalized by the two countries last year. The initial fund is earmarked for a gas-fired combined-cycle power plant project in Encinal, Texas, designed to supply electricity to AI data centers. The investment is intended to demonstrate Korea’s commitment to the economic partnership and help secure the agreed 15 percent tariff ceiling for its key exports. However, the commencement of actual funding has failed to ease U.S. trade pressure. U.S. President Donald Trump has significantly ramped up his rhetoric, publicly pressuring Seoul to join a $54 billion Alaska LNG pipeline and terminal project. item.title: Foreigners armed with blunt weapons clash in Pyeongtaek, Central Asian groups suspected
item.description: Police believe a late-night mass brawl involving foreign nationals in Pyeongtaek, Gyeonggi Province, over the weekend stemmed from a feud between groups from Central Asian countries. On Saturday, police responded to a report at about 11:10 p.m. that several vehicles had gathered and a brawl appeared imminent, but those involved had already dispersed by the time officers arrived. About 30 minutes later, police issued a "Code Zero," the highest dispatch level, after a second report of a gathering of foreign nationals. Police arrested two men in their 20s on the spot as they fled. The two arrested men were identified as Russian and Kyrgyz nationals. Police said they entered Korea on student and other visas. Both men suffered injuries including fractures, and a wooden stick and a baseball bat picked up nearby were left at the scene. Police believe the incident stemmed from a quarrel between groups of Kazakh and Kyrgyz nationals. Authorities are pursuing those still at large. Nearby CCTV footage suggests about 15 people took part, police said. Police have yet to identify the suspects who fled,

item.title: Citizen diplomacy brings Korea, Japan closer
item.description: When you are abroad, you will more often than not find yourself becoming a patriot. Older Koreans say people tend to develop a greater sense of unity and solidarity with their community when they live in a foreign country. Their shared sense of identity often brings them closer together and helps them maintain a strong bond. It is common to see Koreans gather to share happiness, guided by the belief that happiness doubles and sorrow is halved when shared with others. Compared with this sense of unity among people of the same ethnic background, it is relatively uncommon to see people from a different culture throw a party solely to celebrate the achievements of a Korean. The chances are even slimmer when the host is Japanese, given the two countries' long and often contentious history. Such a rare event took place in Houston, Texas, in September. Akemi Saitoh, the wife of Yasuhiko Saitoh, president of Japan's largest chemical company Shin-Etsu, invited some 70 guests — most of them people of Korean descent — to their Houston residence on Sept. 20 for a party celebrating Korean balleri

item.title: S. Korean military launches operation to remove NK mines at recent DMZ blast site
item.description: The South Korean military launched an operation Monday to remove any remaining land mines planted by North Korea at the site of a recent blast inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that left three South Korean service members injured. Three South Korean military officers were injured Sept. 21, two seriously, when two land mines south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) in the western DMZ exploded. Following a joint inspection of the blast site, the United Nations Command (UNC) and South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) concluded that the mines were "highly likely" planted by North Korea and urged Pyongyang to apologize. Seoul has also discovered two additional land mines at and near the blast site. The UNC, which oversees the DMZ, said the latest explosion constituted a violation of the Armistice Agreement that ended the 1950-53 Korean War. North Korea has denied responsibility for the blast, accusing South Korea of fabricating the findings and warning of "immediate and merciless" retaliation if its troops are fired upon.

item.title: Delinquent health insurance premiums owed by foreigners total $27.9 mil.
item.description: Delinquent premiums owed by foreigners and overseas Koreans enrolled in Korea's state health insurance system totaled 37.5 billion won ($27.9 million) as of the end of 2025, a government report showed Monday. According to the National Assembly Budget Office report, unpaid premiums rose 42 percent from 26.4 billion won in 2021, while the number of delinquent households jumped 58.1 percent from 21,728 to 34,349 over the same period. Foreign nationals accounted for the vast majority of delinquent households, with 33,725 owing 34.4 billion won, it said. Over the past five years, 134,505 cases totaling 47.7 billion won have been written off as uncollectible, the report said. Under current law, health insurance benefits are suspended while an insured person is abroad. However, some foreign workers have reportedly left their foreigner registration cards and health insurance eligibility behind when returning home or traveling overseas, allowing people who remain in Korea to use their identities to receive medical treatment. item.title: From samulnori to King Sejong: Korean culture sweeps Vietnam National University
item.description: HANOI — Traditional Korean folk music rang out across the campus of the University of Social Sciences and Humanities at Vietnam National University, Hanoi, Saturday. Samulnori, a traditional Korean percussion performance that has largely disappeared from university campuses in Korea, was brought back to life by Vietnamese students in the heart of a Hanoi campus, performed by students in the Korean language department’s troupe. The performance opened the “Vietnam Central and Northern Universities Korean Language Department Festival,” organized by the Embassy of the Republic of Korea in Vietnam and the Korea Foundation. The festival, which began in 2010, provides Korean language students with opportunities to interact and exchange ideas. The 15 students, dressed in traditional Korean pants and jackets with vests and colorful sashes, each held a traditional drum or gong as they delivered an energetic performance. item.title: Zara Larsson sets Seoul ablaze with 'Midnight Sun' tour
item.description: Zara Larsson, the popstar who rose to fame by winning a Swedish talent show at the young age of 10, is now in the strongest stretch of her career. The Swedish singer won two American Music Awards (AMAs) in May, and "Lush Life," released a decade ago, returned to the Billboard Hot 100 after a fan-dance video went viral. Her fifth album, "Midnight Sun," arrived last year to strong listener reviews and has taken her around the world on a tour of the same name. On Sunday, that tour reached Myunghwa Live Hall in western Seoul for her first-ever headline show in Korea. She had visited only once before, for the 2017 Asia Song Festival. Demand was high enough that a second night was added, and both sold out. For an artist of her current profile, Myunghwa Live Hall, a performance venue with a capacity of about 1,600, is a surprisingly small room, but nobody in it on Sunday night seemed to mind. Many in the crowd were fully glittered and glammed up, flowers in their hair and all, dressed as if the night was a party of their own. item.title: North Korean drama features man preparing meals in floral apron
item.description: A North Korean drama featuring a man preparing a meal has prompted speculation that the scene may be part of efforts to pave the way for the succession of Kim Jong-un’s daughter, Ju-ae. The portrayal of improved status for women in the deeply patriarchal North Korean society is being interpreted as an attempt to bolster Ju-ae, who could potentially become the country’s first female leader. A scene from a North Korean drama showing a man wearing a floral apron and preparing a meal for his wife and daughter drew attention on social media on Sunday. Given that men performing household chores is unusual in North Korea, some observers have suggested that the scene may have been deliberately included with Ju-ae in mind. As there has never been a female supreme leader or successor in North Korea, the scene is being interpreted as an effort to lower the political and cultural barriers Ju-ae could face in the future. item.title: Over 5 mil. resident registration number records leaked in Korea over 6 years
item.description: Resident registration numbers were exposed more than 5.05 million times in personal data breach cases that prompted enforcement action by the Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) and the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) over the past six years, data showed Sunday. According to an analysis by the office of Rep. Han Chang-min of the Social Democratic Party, 130 cases involving the exposure of resident registration numbers were subject to enforcement action between 2021 and September 2026. Excluding three cases for which the scale of the breach could not be determined, the remaining cases involved a combined 5.05 million exposures of resident registration numbers. By institution or company, the National Center for the Rights of the Child accounted for the largest number of resident registration number exposures, with a combined 1.16 million instances across three data breach cases. It was followed by Yanolja with 1 million, NHN Wetoo with 524,620, Lotte Card with 452,313, Duo Information with 427,464 encrypted records and LG Uplus with 297,117 encrypted records. Han's office

item.title: RM reveals art that inspires him at SFMOMA
item.description: SAN FRANCISCO — To millions around the world, Kim Nam-joon is RM, the leader of BTS, as well as a rapper, songwriter and producer. But on the seventh floor of the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA), another side of the global superstar comes into focus as a collector, student of art and curator. For fans of a global superstar accustomed to stadiums filled with screaming crowds, the experience at SFMOMA feels remarkably intimate. Rather than presenting RM the performer, the exhibition offers a glimpse into the objects and artists that have captured his attention in quieter moments. For anyone planning to visit the newly opened "RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me" exhibit in San Francisco, California, be sure to set aside plenty of time, as there is a lot to take in. Visitors will quickly come to understand how personal this exhibit is for RM, as guests are welcomed into the exhibit hall with a giant mural featuring notes and writing about the works in his own hand. From there, spectators move between bold paintings and delicate ceramics to sculpture, textiles and mixed-media work

item.title: 'Even BTS served in military': Debate reignites over athletes' service exemption privilege
item.description: Debate has reignited over the military service exemption for athletes who win medals at international athletic competitions, after some players made remarks gloating about the privilege at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. While the issue has been around for more than a decade, calls for abolishing the system have grown stronger, especially in light of fairness issues with others who contributed to raising national prestige in other fields, including global stars like BTS, and the shrinking population in the age group eligible for military enlistment. The controversy resurfaced after Korea beat host Japan 1-0 in the men's football final on Saturday, winning a fourth consecutive Asian Games title. Afterward, some players brought up the military service exemption in interviews. "I don't think the medal or the trophy mattered at all. The real reward for us is the military exemption, so I think we played with only that in mind," said Yang Min-hyeok, a 20-year-old winger. While the issue has been around for more than a decade, calls for abolishing the system have grown stronger, especially in light of fairness issues with others who contributed to raising national prestige in other fields, including global stars like BTS, and the shrinking population in the age group eligible for military enlistment. The controversy resurfaced after Korea beat host Japan 1-0 in the men's football final on Saturday, winning a fourth consecutive Asian Games title. Afterward, some players brought up the military service exemption in interviews. "I don't think the medal or the trophy mattered at all. The real reward for us is the military exemption, so I think we played with only that in mind," said Yang Min-hyeok, a 20-year-old winger. Lee Gi-hyuk, a 26-year-old defender, smiled as he held up his gold medal to reporters and said, "I'm not going to the military

item.title: Man in 20s arrested for killing elderly stranger in Seoul
item.description: A man in his 20s was arrested Monday on suspicion of killing a man whom he did not know in a residential neighborhood in northern Seoul, police said. The suspect, whose identity was withheld, was caught at around 1 a.m. for allegedly killing a man in his 70s in Gangbuk Ward on Saturday, according to Seoul Gangbuk Police Station. The police discovered the victim's body at around 7 p.m. Saturday while searching for him after receiving a report that he could not be reached. Investigators have so far determined that the two did not know each other prior to the incident. The suspect told the police that the killing was unintentional and occurred after the two got into an argument when their shoulders bumped into each other on the street, sources said. The police plan to seek an arrest warrant for the suspect after investigating the exact circumstances of the incident, including his motive.

item.title: Japan PM calls China 'important neighbor', pledges stable relationship
item.description: TOKYO — Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called China an "important neighbor" and pledged to build a stable relationship between the rival nations in a policy address on Monday. Diplomatic relations between the Asian economic giants have been at rock bottom since Takaichi suggested in November that Tokyo may intervene in any attack on the island of Taiwan, which Beijing claims as its territory. "China is an important neighbor, and despite difficulties, we have built up a long-standing relationship over the years," she told parliament. "We will work to ensure communication on shared challenges, promote dialogue to safeguard our national interests, and build a constructive and stable relationship." But she added that Japan would also "firmly assert our country's positions" and "strongly call for responsible behavior". The premier also signalled her government would draft a comprehensive plan to deal with population decline, which she called a "quietly advancing national crisis". item.title: Korea's delisting drive faces court challenge as expulsions nearly double
item.description: The government's push to speed up the delisting of troubled companies is running into legal resistance, industry officials said Sunday. The challenges threaten to complicate efforts to improve the quality of the country's stock market after the number of firms removed from the Korea Exchange (KRX) nearly doubled this year. The Seoul Southern District Court recently granted injunctions sought by KOSPI-listed JooYonTech and Kosdaq-listed KM Pharmaceutical, blocking the KRX from proceeding with their delistings. "Even taking into account the circumstances cited by the defendant, including the possibility that granting the injunction could delay the capital market reforms currently under way, there is a demonstrated need because delisting could harm the plaintiffs' business operations and even threaten their continued existence," the court said. The KRX moved forward the implementation of higher market-capitalization thresholds — 30 billion won ($22.28 million) for KOSPI companies and 20 billion won for Kosdaq firms — to July this year, earlier than the initial January 2027 schedule. item.title: Lee's growing social media use leads to another diplomatic dispute
item.description: As President Lee Jae Myung steps up his activity on X (formerly Twitter) to address sensitive foreign and domestic issues, he is once again seeing social media comments spilling into a diplomatic dispute — this time with Ukraine, following a row with Israel in April. Lee warned Ukraine on Friday that South Korea would take “additional measures” unless Kyiv acknowledges what Seoul says was an agreement to keep the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) confidential and issues a public apology. The disagreement began after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed in a U.N. General Assembly speech on Sept. 23 that the POWs had been sent to South Korea. They were captured while fighting for Russia and later expressed a desire to resettle in the South. Seoul said the disclosure violated an arrangement intended to protect the men and their families. Ukraine denied that any such agreement existed and described the episode as a diplomatic misunderstanding. item.title: HD Hyundai XiteSolution launches 18-ton electric forklift
item.description: HD Hyundai XiteSolution has launched electric forklifts with lifting capacities of up to 18 tons, expanding electrification into heavy-duty worksites such as shipyards, ports and steel mills. The company said Monday that it recently held a test-drive event for its next-generation electric forklifts at its plant in Eumseong, North Chungcheong Province, where it showcased its new large-model lineup and began mass production. The lineup includes 10- to 18-ton models, following the launch of mid-sized electric forklifts last year. HD Hyundai XiteSolution is the only Korean manufacturer producing electric forklifts with capacities of 10 tons or more. Diesel forklifts have traditionally been used at heavy-duty worksites because of their high power and long operating times. But tighter environmental regulations and growing demand to cut carbon emissions are driving the shift to electric models. HD Hyundai XiteSolution applied high-voltage battery systems and enhanced electric motor performance to deliver work speeds, hill-climbing ability and power comparable to those of diesel models. item.title: What will the next leader of the UN need to get the job done in an increasingly complex world?
item.description: UNITED NATIONS — On Jan. 1, the next United Nations secretary-general will take over an aging organization still controlled by World War II powers. What will the world need from that person? Once a major player in solving conflicts and crises around the world, the 81-year-old institution has been sidelined from the top table in trying to end the wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza. And its precarious financial situation — caused mainly by the billions of dollars the United States owes — has forced major cuts to its humanitarian and development programs where it has remained a key player. The annual global gathering of world leaders at the United Nations that ended last week shed some light on what the next U.N. chief needs to focus on and pursue. In his farewell address to the General Assembly, outgoing Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told global leaders, “The world does not need a weaker United Nations.” “It needs a U.N. strong enough to face the world as it is," he said, “and determined enough to build the world as it should.” But is that even possible? item.title: US arrests woman accused of spying for China on Taiwan leader's family
item.description: LOS ANGELES — A woman accused of spying for China on Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te's son and his family was arrested Sunday in the United States, U.S. and Taiwanese officials said. Wanying Zhang, 34, was detained by the FBI at Los Angeles airport "attempting to depart for China," First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said in an X post. Zhang is accused of acting as an unregistered agent of China and spying on a "close relative of a Taiwanese government official" in the United States, Essayli said. The woman allegedly surveilled Lai's "son and his family — filming their home, vehicles, and reporting information back to (People's Republic of China) handlers," the FBI said on its rapid response account on X. China claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex the island. Zhang traveled to Seattle in 2025 and, acting at the direction of Chinese officials, sent "photos, videos, and license plate information to those officials," Essayli said. item.description: Model and actress Jang Yoon-joo has moved to the United Kingdom with her family after her husband decided to pursue graduate studies there. After years of deliberation, Jang decided to accompany him, saying she hopes to find something she can devote herself to in her new surroundings. A video titled “Jang Yoon-joo’s Family Comes to the U.K. After Three Years of Deliberation. Please Take Good Care of Us” was posted on Jang’s YouTube channel, Yoonjure Jang Yoon-joo, on Saturday. The family’s move to the U.K. began about three years ago, when Jang’s husband, Jung Seung-min, expressed a desire to return to school. item.title: Hana Financial Group opens new Incheon HQ, bets on closer finance-tech ties
item.description: Hana Financial Group has announced the completion of its Hana Financial Town project in Cheongna, Incheon, with the opening of a new headquarters, the group said Sunday. The group began developing the complex in 2012, opening an integrated data center in 2017 and a global training campus in 2019. The new 15-story headquarters marks the final stage of the project. At an opening ceremony, Friday, it outlined plans to reshape its workspace and working culture around greater communication and collaboration. About 2,200 employees from the group and 10 major affiliates have been relocating into the building since September. Including staff at the existing data center, the site will house over 4,000 financial and technology professionals. By bringing business units and IT teams into closer proximity, Hana Financial aims to strengthen internal collaboration across banking, data and digital operations, as well as speed up the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). “The opening of the Cheongna headquarters marks the culmination of the Hana Financial Town project and the beginning of a new phas

item.title: AMRO revises up Korean economy's growth projection this year to 3.3%
item.description: An economic surveillance organization in Asia on Monday projected South Korea's economy will expand 3.3 percent this year, revising up its previous forecast of 3.1 percent. The ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) made the assessment in its quarterly update report, without further elaborating on the reasons for the revision from its July forecast. For 2027, the organization expected Asia's No. 4 economy to grow 2.7 percent, compared with its previous estimate of 2.2 percent. Touching on inflation, the agency expected consumer prices to rise 2.7 percent on-year in 2026, compared with its previous forecast of 2.6 percent. For 2027, the inflation forecast was revised down from 2.4 percent to 2.3 percent. Last month, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) raised its 2026 economic growth forecast for Korea to 3.7 percent, citing the country's robust exports. The Paris-based organization's prediction marks a 1.1 percentage-point increase from the 2.6 percent forecast in its June report. item.title: Korea to launch $3.5 bil. frontier AI project next year
item.description: Korea will launch a state-backed project next year to develop a frontier artificial intelligence (AI) model capable of competing with leading Chinese open-source models, with the government planning to make 4.7 trillion won ($3.48 billion) of equity investment in what could be a special purpose company involving the country’s top AI model developers. During a press conference Friday, Second Vice Minister of Science and ICT Ryu Je-myung also said the ongoing national AI foundation model project, which drew significant attention as a competition to develop Korea’s most capable homegrown AI model, will proceed as planned, but its focus will shift toward models tailored to specific industries and real-world applications. "The frontier AI project will begin next year," he said. "It will be reflected in next year's budget, and we will pursue a higher goal by breaking through current technological limitations." item.title: Saudi crude share of S. Korea's imports falls below 30% for 1st time in 5 years
item.description: Saudi Arabian crude oil accounted for less than 30 percent of South Korea's crude imports this year, industry data showed Monday, amid efforts by local refiners to diversify their sources of crude following geopolitical risks in the Middle East. According to the data from the Korea National Oil Corp. and the Korea Petroleum Association, Saudi crude accounted for 29.9 percent of the country's total crude oil imports in the January-August period, down from 30.91 percent in the previous month. It marked the first time in five years that the share fell below the 30 percent mark. Saudi Arabia remains South Korea's largest source of crude oil. The annual share of Saudi crude last fell below the 30 percent level in 2021, when global crude oil supplies were disrupted amid heightened tensions in the Middle East and the COVID-19 pandemic. If the downward trend continues, Saudi Arabia's share could fall to third place or lower this year, potentially surpassing the previous low recorded in 1986, according to industry officials. item.title: Arrests of drug smugglers, manufacturers rise 33.8% this year: police
item.description: The number of people arrested for drug smuggling and manufacturing rose more than 30 percent in the first eight months of this year from a year earlier, police said Monday. The National Office of Investigation (NOI) under the Korean National Police Agency said it arrested 174 people for drug manufacturing and smuggling between January and August, up 33.8 percent from 130 during the same period last year. The number of people arrested for dealing drugs also rose 6.6 percent on-year to 3,396 during the cited period. The total number of people caught for drug-related offenses stood at 9,530, up 5.3 percent from a year earlier. Of the total, 706 people were arrested for offenses involving medical drugs, an 11.9 percent increase from a year earlier. The police have focused their investigative efforts on cutting off drug supply sources and distribution networks this year. item.title: Trump faces midterm verdict as Democrats close in on US Congress
item.description: WASHINGTON — A month before the US midterms, Democrats are eyeing control of Congress -- and the power to put President Donald Trump on the defensive for the rest of his term by investigating his administration and stalling his agenda. The November 3 vote is shaping up as a verdict on one of the most turbulent presidencies in US history -- and, by several measures, Trump goes into it less popular than any predecessor facing midterms in modern polling. Americans will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 senators, alongside governors in 36 states. The election decides who controls the legislature -- which passes laws, sets the budget and polices the White House. Forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 75 percent chance of winning the House, projecting a 234-201 majority. It rates the Senate a near coin flip, with Democrats narrowly favored to take it 51-49. Control of the House alone would hand Democrats powerful committees and subpoena authority. item.title: Fishing boat capsizes off Jeju; 9 rescued, 2 missing
item.description: A fishing boat carrying 11 people capsized in waters off the southern resort island of Jeju on Monday, with nine people rescued and two others missing, authorities said. The 29-ton coastal longline fishing boat capsized in waters about 65 kilometers northwest of Chagwi Island at 3:04 a.m., according to the Jeju Coast Guard. Nearby fishing boats rescued nine foreign crew members — eight Indonesians and one Vietnamese. The rescued crew members were found to be in stable condition. Two others — the Korean captain and one Indonesian crew member — remain missing, according to the Coast Guard. Authorities dispatched helicopters and patrol vessels to the scene to conduct search and rescue operations. One Navy vessel and several civilian fishing boats have also been mobilized, it added. The cause of the accident has not yet been determined. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook ordered authorities to mobilize all available personnel and equipment to prioritize rescue efforts. item.title: Kia ranks 2nd in Jan.-Aug. auto sales in Britain on strong demand for Sportage SUV
item.description: Kia Motors Corp.'s sales in Britain ranked second in the January-August period, helped by strong demand for its Sportage sport utility vehicle (SUV), industry data showed Monday. According to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, the Korean automaker sold 76,850 vehicles in Britain during the eight-month period, up 2.3 percent from the same period last year. Kia ranked second behind Volkswagen, which sold 111,830 vehicles, the data showed. Kia was the only Asian automaker to rank among Britain's top five sellers during the period, moving up one spot from a year earlier and surpassing European brands, such as BMW and Audi. Kia's sales in Britain have steadily increased, surpassing 100,000 units for four consecutive years. Its annual sales came to 100,191 vehicles in 2022, 107,765 in 2023, 112,252 in 2024 and 113,436 in 2025. If the strong sales trend continues through the end of this year, Kia's annual sales in Britain are expected to surpass the 100,000 mark for the fifth straight year and set a new annual sales record. item.title: Lee's approval rating dips after 2-week rise: poll
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung's approval rating fell slightly last week following a two-week rise, a poll showed Monday. In the poll conducted on 2,515 adults nationwide from last Monday through Friday, positive assessments of Lee's job performance stood at 37.4 percent, down 0.5 percentage point from the previous week, Realmeter said. Negative assessments also dropped 0.3 percentage point to 59.8 percent, while 2.8 percent of respondents said they were unsure. Lee's approval rating had risen for two consecutive weeks, helped by his clarification of key political issues during a press conference on Sept. 18. "The announcement of livelihood and welfare policies using excess tax revenue served as a positive factor this week. But personnel, security and livelihood-related negative factors appear to have had a greater impact," Realmeter said. Negative factors included a controversy over the establishment of new investigative agencies — the Serious Crimes Investigation Agency (SCIA) and the Prosecution Service — and the appointment of the SCIA chief, as well as the recent land mine blast inside

item.title: US withdraws all bomber planes from UK airbase: Pentagon
item.description: WASHINGTON — The Pentagon confirmed reports Sunday that the United States has withdrawn all B-1 bomber planes from Royal Air Force Fairford, the UK airbase where a suspicious incident triggered nearby evacuations. A statement from a Pentagon official said "we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States." The statement noted that "operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time." Police were called to the base in southwest England last Sunday after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in "suspicious" activity. The scare forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used to launch strikes on Iran. Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel thievery, as energy prices in the U.K. hit record highs this week. Investigators said they did not find any explosives in the vans, but instead "a quantity of petrol was recovered," National Counter Terrorism Policing head Lawren

item.title: Extreme heat putting pregnant women, newborns at risk: UN climate chief
item.description: NADI, Fiji — Extreme heat is putting pregnant mothers and their newborns at increasing risk, United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell will warn on Monday. Speaking at the "pre-COP" summit in Nadi, Fiji, Stiell will cite a new survey showing more than two thirds of health professionals across five continents had seen complications caused by intense heat in the past five years. "Rising temperatures mean rising danger in pregnancy," he is expected to say. "Climate-driven extreme heat during pregnancy is increasingly linked to premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight, and maternal complications." "The picture is clear and very disturbing: as extreme heat worsens, pregnancy and birth are now a new faultline in the global climate crisis, and one which is potentially fatal," Stiell will say. "This faultline must not become another deep chasm of climate-driven suffering, inequality and injustice." Scientists warn that climate change is making extreme weather events more intense and resulting in heat records tumbling more often. Around 33 countries, spanning from western Europe to the Sahel

item.title: Brazil election headed to runoff, projection shows, as Bolsonaro lead narrows
item.description: BRASILIA/SAO PAULO/RIO DE JANEIRO — Senator Flavio Bolsonaro held a narrowing lead in the first round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, after more than half the votes were counted, with pollster Datafolha projecting that the election would proceed to a second vote. Flavio, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro who hopes to return his father's right-wing movement to power, was leading leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, 80, who is seeking a fourth term, following a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of U.S. meddling. With about 65 percent of votes reported, Flavio led Lula with 49.58 percent of the votes to the president's 42.25 percent. A candidate must pass 50 percent in order to win outright in the first round. The two leading candidates were expected to head into a second round vote, Brazilian pollster Datafolha said. item.title: Underground show brings together 11 bands in Sinchon
item.description: A show at western Seoul's top punk venue Baby Doll brings together 11 bands Saturday. The expansive, diverse and yet reasonably affordable show is also Matthew Gamble's debut as a promoter. "A lot of people in the underground punk and hardcore scene in Korea have also been asking me to put on shows for a while, so eventually everything just collided together," he said. Gamble, the proprietor behind streetwear brand Diazable, has been working hard to promote Korea's underground scene for several years now. He can often be seen at shows filming the bands for his YouTube channel, Diazable Music Breakdown. "I’ve filmed every band on this first show in some capacity," he said. "That made it a lot easier to approach them because I’d already had some kind of interaction with them before. I wasn’t just some random person suddenly asking them to play a show." item.title: Anamaría Oramas ushers sounds of contemporary Colombian jazz to Korea
item.description: Breaking free from more familiar Latin American jazz sounds like tango and bossa nova, musician Anamaría Oramas is set to introduce her own traditional and contemporary Colombian jazz crossover sounds to Korea. The singer and instrumentalist is scheduled to perform at the Jarasum Jazz Festival in Gapyeong, Gyeonggi Province, happening Oct. 9-11. The annual music festival, now on its 23rd edition, is one of the leading jazz events in the country and has featured jazz musicians from all over the world since its inception in 2004. She’s also making appearances in Seoul live venues Jazz Club Janus, Subriot and Morene Sukha as part of her 10th anniversary world tour. Through her parents’ encouragement to pursue a career in music, Oramas trained as a classical musician in her younger years and developed a love affair with wind instruments. item.title: Lee calls for breaking off from 'vicious cycle of hostility' for peace
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung on Sunday called for breaking off from "a vicious cycle of hostility and confrontation to create a virtuous cycle of peace and prosperity," in a speech marking the anniversary of a declaration aimed at improving inter-Korean relations. "The journey to resolve the Korean Peninsula issue and establish peace will not be easy. But it is clear that is the road we have to walk," Lee said in remarks read out by Vice Unification Minister Kim Nam-jung. His remarks came on the 19th anniversary of the Oct. 4 Inter-Korean Declaration signed by late former President Roh Moo-hyun and late North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, the father of current North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, in 2007. The president called the declaration a "historic agreement" on transitioning inter-Korean relations to one of mutual trust and moving forward together toward a permanent peace system. "Unfortunately, as the promise for peace and prosperity was not fulfilled, hostility and confrontation filled that space," he said. item.title: From 'Coffee Prince' to 'My Lovely Sam Soon,' 2000s K-drama fashion is back
item.description: After years of playful, edgy Y2K fashion dominating wardrobes, young Korean women are turning toward something decidedly more grown-up. The so-called "grown woman look," a Korean fashion trend centered on sophisticated, understated femininity, is gaining traction among women in their 20s and 30s. Fashion brands are responding with fall and winter collections built around polished silhouettes, richer colors and restrained styling. According to the fashion industry, the trend marks a shift away from the bold, youthful aesthetic associated with the Y2K revival. Instead, consumers are gravitating toward looks that appear effortless yet refined, with a relaxed and restrained mood. Deep colors, subtle femininity and clean silhouettes are among the defining elements. The trend has even revived interest in the wardrobes of female characters from Korean TV shows that aired nearly two decades ago. item.title: Endless search for graves of forgotten independence fighters
item.description: At a ceremony held at Incheon International Airport's Terminal 1 on Nov. 15, 2022, to repatriate the remains of independence fighters buried overseas, the voice of Hwang So-young, the great-great-granddaughter of independence fighter Lee Han-ho (1895-1960), trembled slightly as she reached the final lines of a letter she had written to him. Until then, she had read it in a calm, steady voice. Moments later, Lee's remains were carried into the ceremony hall by an honor guard from the Ministry of National Defense's ceremonial unit. It was his return home, 107 years after leaving his homeland. Lee moved to China's Jiandao region in 1915 and joined Maenghodan, an anti-Japanese independence group. After participating in a March 1 Independence Movement demonstration in 1919, he fled to Russia and then Shanghai, China, to escape Japanese police. He later moved to Switzerland, where he continued his independence movement activities. He died there in September 1960. item.title: Meet Issa Amro: Palestinian Human Rights Advocate Attacked by Settlers, Detained by Israeli Army
item.description:
We speak with Palestinian human rights defender Issa Amro after he was detained at an Israeli military base for seven hours on Friday. Amro, the founder of the Hebron-based group Youth Against Settlements, was helping a Palestinian family that he says had been attacked by armed Israeli settlers at their farmhouse outside Hebron in the occupied West Bank. Amro says when Israeli soldiers arrived, they ignored the settlers and instead targeted the Palestinians, including him. Amro tells Democracy Now! that soldiers handcuffed and blindfolded him before transporting him to the base in the back of a military vehicle. He was freed after an international outcry over his arrest.

“What happened to me is happening to many Palestinian families and many Palestinian human rights defenders and many Palestinian journalists,” says Amro. “It’s not the first time. It’s not the last time. We have to keep working to make occupation [and] apartheid costly and make this kind of human rights violation costly for the offenders.”

item.title: "I Am Jane Doe": Cornell Case Reignites Debate over Rape Culture, Frats & Prosecuting Sex Crimes
item.description:
Revelations of sexual assault at a Cornell University fraternity in 2024 and how the university responded have sparked national outrage, reigniting a public debate about “the extent to which fraternities, the extent to which athletics really support this kind of culture that allows perpetrators to escape with little or no accountability,” says law professor Deborah Tuerkheimer.

In 2024, seven male students avoided criminal prosecution after allegedly drugging and gang-raping a female student at the Chi Phi fraternity house. Cornell is now under intense scrutiny for its handling of the original investigation, which found that the student identified as Jane Doe was sexually assaulted by two of seven men, resulting in expulsions for two and lesser consequences for the other five. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has admitted that his office at the time did not independently investigate the case when it declined to bring charges. The DA has now reopened the case, and New York Governor Kathy Hochul has named Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to investigate how the case was handled.

“Around the country, we see a pattern of investigators, police officers and even prosecutors deciding at the outset that the allegations are not worth pursuing, and dismissing the case before any kind of investigation gets off the ground,” says Tuerkheimer.

item.title: Far Right Makes Gains in Brazil as Flávio Bolsonaro Tops Lula in First Round of Presidential Race
item.description:
Brazil’s presidential election is headed to a runoff between leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro after neither candidate cleared 50% in Sunday’s vote, in which the right made gains in Congress and in governor races across the country. Bolsonaro received 47% of the vote compared to Lula’s 45%. The second round of voting is on October 25. If elected, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to grant amnesty to his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest and serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup in 2022 to overturn Lula’s last victory. He has also vowed to strengthen ties to the Trump administration, which is accused of trying to influence the result in Bolsonaro’s favor.

“The momentum has been with the right since 2018,” says Brazilian philosopher Rodrigo Nunes, who explains that public disillusionment with politics is part of that shift. “Lots of people see the far right as promising them, 'Well, if this is all there is, if all we can expect from the future is ever more dog-eat-dog conditions, an ever more competitive struggle of all against all, at least what the far right says is the state will get off our backs.'”

Nunes is author of Neither Vertical nor Horizontal: A Theory of Political Organization and the new book Anatomy of Disintegration: What Brazil Reveals About the Global Far Right. He recently wrote about the stakes of the Brazilian election for North South Notes.

item.title: Trump confirms national intelligence chief as new AI czar
item.description: WASHINGTON, United States — US President Donald Trump on Sunday confirmed national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as head of a new White House task force on artificial intelligence, amid increasingly vocal warnings from researchers about the technology's potential dangers. Under Clayton, the new Super Intelligence Force -- Trump's preferred term for artificial intelligence -- will ensure that the United States "continue to lead the world" in AI development, the president posted on his Truth Social platform. Trump said the force had also been tasked to "protect the interests, and improve the lives of all Americans." Clayton will become the second person to hold the informal title after venture capitalist David Sacks, who held the role at the start of Trump's second term before stepping down. Sacks continues to advise the president on AI, as does Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Trump said last month he would create an AI force modeled on the Space Force he established during his first term, and name a czar to coordinate federal efforts. item.title: Pro-Ukraine governing coalition wins 35% in Latvian election
item.description: RIGA, Latvia — Latvian lawmakers on Sunday planned to begin negotiations to form a new government following a parliamentary election in which pro-Ukraine Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs 's four-party coalition emerged with 35% of the vote. A political crisis in May over the handling of stray drones suspected of coming from Ukraine brought down the governing coalition that had been under strain over several other issues. The parliament, or Saeima, then approved the coalition led by Kulbergs of the centrist United List party, previously in opposition. Latvia, like its Baltic neighbors Lithuania and Estonia, strongly supports Ukraine in its fight against Moscow’s invasion. It borders both Russia and Moscow-allied Belarus. Saturday's vote came as the small republic on NATO’s eastern flank contends with growing concern about potential Russian aggression . The election saw a voter turnout above 51%, according to election data. Nearly 1.56 million people in the nation of more than 1.8 million were entitled to choose the 100 members of the single-chamber Saeima for a four-year term. The Unit

item.title: Cornell president vows review in wake of alleged student gang rape
item.description: NEW YORK — The president of Cornell University voiced support Saturday for an external review of the institution facing widespread outcry over the alleged gang rape of a student in 2024. The incident was detailed in a graphic lawsuit filed last month, drawing harsh backlash against the Ivy League institution and New York prosecutors for not filing any criminal charges against the accused perpetrators. "In conjunction with our board of trustees, I welcome the independent review by an outside law firm into all aspects of Cornell's handling of the 2024 matter," President Michael Kotlikoff said in a video shared on Cornell's website. The plaintiff claimed in the civil suit that she was drugged with ketamine, assaulted and raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, a social club for male students. "This has been one of the most difficult weeks in our history, and I know many of you are angry, saddened, and struggling," Kotlikoff continued. "What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come." The criminal investigation into

item.title: Personal data of some 24,000 KEPCO employees leaked
item.description: The personal information of some 24,000 employees at the state-run Korea Electric Power Corp. (KEPCO) has been leaked, the company said Sunday, the latest in a series of personal data leaks at corporations. "We became aware that the personal information of employees was exposed on an external web site at around 3:59 p.m. Thursday," KEPCO said in a statement. The leaked information includes their names, job positions and telephone numbers but does not include sensitive information, such as their resident registration numbers, the company added. KEPCO said in the statement it has since notified affected employees and completed deleting the leaked information at around midnight Friday. Customer information, stored in a separate system, was not compromised. The case comes after several major financial firms, including Hana Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and Shinhan Bank, recently suffered back-to-back leaks of customer information in hacking attacks. A KEPCO official said the company is verifying the exact cause of the incident and that the data leak appears to be unrelated to artificial intelligence (

item.title: German Korean disco-punk band returns to Seoul
item.description: Korean German musician Ja-min Oh has returned to Korea, the land of her parents, several times over her life. But it took an encounter with Rumkicks, a band of spiky-haired girl punks from Seoul, to connect her band, disco-punk duo Minoh, with the music scene here. Oh was stage manager at Pit Rock, a venue in the small western city of Aachen, when Rumkicks stopped by to play a festival on May 24, 2025. She started a conversation with Heynam Sin, who was filling in for Rumkicks on bass at the time, and Sin gave her a personal connection with the local scene. Shortly after, Oh and her bandmate Guido Kloppisch went on holiday to Seoul. "A friend put us in touch with Club Victim — they said yes, and we played as a two-piece on instruments we rented at Nakwon Music Arcade," Oh said. An online video of the impromptu show reached the Tokyo venue Ruby Room. The venue sent an invite, but the two Minoh members were already back in Germany so they couldn't play. "None of this was planned," Oh said. "Now, one year later, it is — and this whole DIY accident somehow ended up funded by the Goethe-I

item.title: Germany's Merz visits Kyiv as Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian cities
item.description: KYIV, Ukraine — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv Sunday in a show of support as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukrainian cities. The aerial war has intensified, with Moscow menacing cities across Ukraine with hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones , while Kyiv has been striking Russia’s oil industry and businesses . Merz said he traveled to Kyiv, his second trip as chancellor, to demonstrate Germany’s support for Ukraine. “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said in a statement Sunday, adding that he told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, “You can continue to count on our help.” Merz said the partnership between the two countries was “not a one-way street,” pointing to German and Ukrainian companies jointly developing technologies that benefit both sides. “This makes us safer and stronger,” he said. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the agenda would focus on "strengthening Ukraine, our defense and resilience, and our shared European security.” Russia’s Foreig

item.title: Iran not to reopen Strait of Hormuz until conditions are met, Nournews reports
item.description: DUBAI — The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met, Nournews reported Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf as saying on Sunday, a few days after Tehran received Washington's reply to its diplomatic proposal. “The Americans, who say something different in the media, have recently put forward proposals through a mediator. But they must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over," Qalibaf was quoted as saying. "The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met."

item.title: Police officer arrested over AI-generated sexual deepfakes
item.description: A police officer has been arrested last month for allegedly generating sexually exploitative deepfakes of people he knew with the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and sharing them on Telegram, police said Sunday. According to police, the officer, assigned to Dongdaemun Police Station in Seoul, was arrested Sept. 16 on charges including possessing sexual abuse material and sexually explicit deepfakes, as well as creating and distributing such content. Investigators found some 5,600 images and videos in his possession, including about 2,600 deepfakes, 1,600 pieces of child and adolescent sexual abuse material and 1,300 illegally filmed videos. Police also suspect that he personally created and distributed some of the illicit content. The case came to light during an investigation by the Busan Metropolitan Police Agency into a Telegram chat room where sexually explicit deepfakes were allegedly being shared. item.title: Stray Kids follows BTS in Grammy boycott over Asian pop category
item.description: K-pop group Stray Kids is boycotting next year’s Grammys, following BTS in its decision not to submit music for consideration amid mounting controversy over the award show's newly created Asian pop category. The BBC reported on Friday that JYP Entertainment, the boyband's agency, confirmed that the group did not submit any music for consideration for the 69th Grammy Awards. "Stray Kids did not submit for the Grammys," the agency was quoted as saying. The decision came less than a day after the Recording Academy, which organizes the Grammys, announced that it would move forward with its Best Asian Pop Music Performance category. Stray Kids has been considered a leading contender for the new award, given the group’s strong presence in the global music market. The group has topped the Billboard 200 nine times, the second-highest tally for any group after The Beatles. All eight members also hold voting membership in the Recording Academy, underscoring their growing presence in the U.S. music industry. item.title: ADHD drug prescriptions surge 38% in 2 years
item.description: Prescriptions for methylphenidate, an attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) treatment widely known as "study drug" among students in Korea, have surged nearly 38 percent over the past two years in the country and are especially high among people aged 19 and under, data showed Sunday. According to the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety and the Korea Institute of Drug Safety and Risk Management, 58.05 million methylphenidate tablets were prescribed in the first half of this year, up 12.1 percent from the same period a year earlier. This marked a 37.8 percent increase from the first half of 2024, when 42.13 million tablets were prescribed. Methylphenidate is a controlled medical substance in Korea and needs a doctor's prescription to be purchased. Alarming is that methylphenidate prescriptions were particularly high among people aged 19 and under, who accounted for about half of the total. In the first half of this year, 28.81 million tablets were prescribed to people in the age group. Males accounted for 20.9 million tablets, far more than the 7.91 million prescribed to females. Pres

item.title: Lee orders thorough probe into data breaches at local banks
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung on Sunday ordered a thorough investigation into a string of recent data breaches at financial institutions, as artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cyberattacks increasingly target them. According to Cheong Wa Dae, Lee was briefed on recent data breaches at financial and public institutions and their responses to the incidents. "The president ordered officials to conduct a thorough investigation and make every effort to devise measures, with a grave awareness of the seriousness of the matter," presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said. The remarks came after a series of data breaches at major financial firms over the past several days. Shinhan Bank on Thursday reported a breach affecting about 25,000 customers, followed by similar incidents reported at KB Kookmin Bank, Hana Bank and BNK Busan Bank on Friday. The leaked information included customers' names and phone numbers, as well as annual income and loan limits. Some customers' resident registration numbers were also exposed. The breaches have since spread beyond major banks to nonbank financial institutions.
